stories.title_en: AI made self-hosting fun again
stories.title_ja: AI made self-hosting fun again

comments.author: cliche
comments.text: > When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place. Wish I had this restraint. I’ve been vibing everything I can think of. It’s got to the point I made a small platform on top of k3s so that the agent can yolo deploy into a homeserver behind Tailscale. Once deployed it becomes natural selection for which vibes live and which die. Solo vibey self hosting llm usage - bliss. Corporate agentic engineering working with others - soul crushing.

comments.author: jjcm
comments.text: In some ways it's better, in some ways it's worse. It's certainly easier than ever to spin up a VPS/cloudflare proxy and deploy. Agents can pretty much do that end to end. The bigger issue is you're then accountable for keeping up with security. Previously that meant using fail2ban and running a system update every few months. Now it means patching within 24hrs of a CVE9+ dropping, which is happening at an accelerated rate. It got so bad during October I made https://firefighter.sh/ as a joke (a root-permissioned agent that continuously monitors for CVEs and patches your system live as soon as they drop - it's a security nightmare given the nondeterministic aspect of AI), but I'm actually starting to come around to the idea for my non-critical servers.

comments.author: jlengrand
comments.text: AI made self-hosting fun again for sure, for self-made tools or getting home assistant dashboards done in no time. But it mostly has made it scary as ever honestly. I've had a home server since forever, but with the sheer amount of CVEs lately I've been breached twice over the past year; and I've also been constantly hammered by bot traffic. Synology has had several zero days too in the past months. Self-hosting is fun, but behind a triple reinforced wall.

comments.author: n4bz0r
comments.text: > For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time). > I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary. Both of these cases are a great fit for Ansible or the alternatives. Given how much the author leans towards the idea of storing configuration in repos, it's a bit odd I haven't seen a single mention of configuration management tools. Generate Ansible playbooks, set up a simple CI/CD workflow and you don't need an agent to do the same manual labor every time - it just needs to bump the versions and make a PR/push. Saves a great deal of tokens. I have a feeling that AI prices are only going to go up and such 'frivolous' usage when agents repeat a lot of unnecessary actions is going to become an anti-pattern (unless you have unlimited funds).

comments.author: velo_aprx
comments.text: With AI, the problem-solving aspect of my interest in computers is gone. And with it, much of my interest in computers. The fact that AI can do pretty much anything is amazing, but using it feels about as rewarding as using cheat codes in your favorite game as a kid. It's great fun for a while, until you realize you've ruined the game for yourself.

stories.title_ja: AMD-specific fork of llama.cpp

comments.author: rao-v
comments.text: Early in 2025 a bunch of folks realized that AMD made a bunch of cards with mediocre compute but incredibly fast HBM2 memory in their circa 2018 gfx906 datacenter series, so you could get 32GB VRAM capable of incredible 1 TB / s bandwidth for $200 (the closest in today’s cards is north of $3000) There has been a rich little ecosystem of folks optimizing llama.cpp for these odd cards (no tensor cores, no native bf16 etc.) including my little personal repo https://github.com/kinchahoy/llama-of-vega.cpp . Stuff like this focused on more modern RDNA doesn’t help us at all. It’s been interesting to see how much each new frontier model can figure out in terms of optimizing for these GPUs and what they can’t! Fable and Astra will regularly run out of ideas until I point them to someone’s actually thoughtful repo and then they’ll diligently incorporate ideas. The optimization wins are huge (I was initially skeptical that per model kernel optimizations would be worth much). 27B at a pristine Q8 quant goes from base llama.cpp at some 250 pp / 25 tg to 600 pp / 40 tg even before speculative decoding.

comments.author: dofm
comments.text: I saw some blurb a while ago that described llama.cpp as a “model zoo”, which is a great description of its utility and generality. In the last couple of days I have been playing with Erik Paperniuk’s M1 port of Inco’s Splash, which has completely transformed the speed of Qwen 3.8 27B and Inkling 2 Mini; it has essentially tripled the speed of the former and more than doubled the speed of the latter. This means the Qwen model is fully viable on an M1 Max, where before I had found it a bit of a waiting game. And it arguably transforms the utility of Inkling 2 Mini; extra speed means it can be left to reason for longer, the downside of needing to do more tool use for search to patch its knowledge is reduced, and it provides a good rough chat model (though this is not its area of greatest strength). I have not yet found anything that can boost Muse Glimmer to the same extent; I would still prefer that. But for me I now find that only the rather slow prefill speed really holds the M1 Max back; I suspect these new custom kernels have made the M5 Pro Mac Mini a really cost-effective option if you want to tinker with local AI.

comments.author: malicz
comments.text: I have a r9700 card and I highly recommend the radiance engine. With a single card it processes (prefill) at 2400 tok/s and decodes at 150 tok/s. With a 4-bit model that is intelligently quantised to have a KLD of 0.006 and top-1 of 0.972 I have been working this engine for a month, throwing a lot of agentic and coding work and it has been doing great! I can run 3 concurrent agent streams all with a 200k context, entirely in vram. EDIT: model: Qwen3.8-27b - https://codeberg.org/StillDeadcode/radiance

comments.author: fiddlerwoaroof
comments.text: I have a MI100, and I managed to get Claude to double or triple the performance of Qwen3.8 by aggressively optimizing the AMD code and porting some of the Nvidia kernels to ROCm: https://github.com/fwoar-greenhouse/vicuna.cpp I've been running this for a while and it seems pretty stable, plus I had Claude validate the ported kernels against the originals to make sure they were reasonably close numerically to the validated implementations.

comments.author: rsolva
comments.text: Interesting! I have had Claude improve llama.cpp the last few days to get Inkling 2 Mini to fly on my 7900XTX, the improvement has been dramatic both for decode and prefill! https://forge.dmz.skyfritt.net/ruben/llama-inkling-2-mini

stories.title_en: The need for a formally verifiable mainstream programming language
stories.title_ja: The need for a formally verifiable mainstream programming language

comments.author: hresvelgr
comments.text: "Beware of bugs in the above code; I have only proved it correct, not tried it." — Donald Knuth Formal correctness does not guarantee desired function. People have written TLA+ specs for their software[1] and not have it materially improve the quality or reliability. You cannot just throw formal verification at a problem. I am very much of the opinion that crap code is an issue of organisation and aesthetics, and that can be automated. This is something that is enforced by frameworks, and despite the popular consensus that LLMs are good at frameworks because of training data, I make another argument that LLMs are good at them because frameworks massively restrict the possibility space of code that can exist and enforce a consistent organisation and aesthetic. The solution as I see it is to make more restrictive frameworks that have a higher chance of producing desired functionality, then afterward we can worry about correctness. [1] https://jepsen.io/analyses/particledb-1.1.4

comments.author: spankalee
comments.text: Wow, I feel like Blaine is describe a language a lot like the one I'm working on now, Zena: https://zena-lang.dev/ I started Zena from wanting a TypeScript-like syntax that compiled to very efficient WebAssembly GC, and AssemblyScript had issues... The motivation for targeting Wasm was as a good sandboxing and orchestration unit for AI-generated code. So, out of both general PL curiosity and enthusiasm, and an attempt to make a language that's good for AI generation, I started adding what I thought were the best features from other languages with a lot of focus on correctness, structure, and optimizability: pattern matching with exhaustiveness checking, ADTs and sum types via sealed classes, value types, async cancelation / structured concurrency, ownership and borrow checking for resources, unicode safe strings, and recently I added runtime contracts and I'll start on refinement types and some kind of proof system soon. The idea is exactly to take a mainstream and familiar-looking language and add more cutting-edge and academic features that help with software correctness. I wrote about some of this here, though not the formal methods parts: https://zena-lang.dev/blog/2026/09/languages-for-the-ai-era/

comments.author: nylonstrung
comments.text: I firmly believe that Lean is already the language OP wants There's lots of progress being made towards compilation to WASM and LLVM, as well as interop with Rust and other languages

comments.author: thomasahle
comments.text: Rather than migrating all code to some new program language, I've been building ProgLib: https://github.com/thomasnormal/proglib which is like "MathLib for Programming". It allows you to import code from any programming language (So far, Python, C++, Rust, and SystemVerilog are partially supported,) and prove stuff about it in Lean. You don't need a "verifiable programming language". All you need is formalized semantics for the programming language you are already using.

comments.author: porcoda
comments.text: Dafny, SPARK Ada, Why3, Verus, Frama-C, TLA+, etc. are all sort of in this direction for different languages and styles of verification. It is nice to see them getting attention now that LLMs make them digestible for a broader set of programmers. I'm not sure one can start with a goal of creating a "mainstream" language that is verification-oriented. Mainstreamness comes from adoption. I'd look at those past languages (like the ones I listed), and ask "why did these not go mainstream" or "why did they not see broad adoption", and try some new ideas to address their gaps to see if a new one will catch on. But the "mainstream" part seems backwards as the goal - if it’s verifiable, ergonomic, flexible, and accessible, maybe it will go mainstream.

stories.title_en: European Commission Declares Browser Competition a Digital Markets Act Priority
stories.title_ja: European Commission Declares Browser Competition a Digital Markets Act Priority

comments.author: Ungh
comments.text: This is a really big thing. One of the things that really pisses me off with iOS at the moment is Safari is terrible. I mean I'm getting rendering errors just filling in this text box. And it doesn't get any better if you add another browser at the moment as it's still WebKit underneath. If there is no competition then there's no reason to fix all this crap in WebKit. And there needs to be alternative ecosystems like Firefox where you can still get usable full-features plugins that kill off ads and allow you to customise your browser.

comments.author: nchmy
comments.text: This is of utmost importance. To the Apple sycophants and those who hate Chromium's dominance: no one is trying to take anything away from you. All that is desired is for any browser to be able to ship their full version on iOS rather than just a skin over Safari. If you want to use Safari still, great! But you'd also be able to use real Firefox, Vivaldi, Ladybird or anything else. This would also allow organizations and app developers - who often provide crucial social and civil services - to finally have the capabilities that they need to provide competent PWAs on iOS, which isn't generally possible because of how deliberately hobbled they are there - especially the install process, which is a requirement in order to access important APIs as well as have more robust persisted storage. Without this, developers are hesitant to build PWAs at all because a primary demographic is largely inaccessible. comments.text: There is a reason why these inference wrappers exist, it’s a way to arbitrage compute. Imagine, some team or individual has a way to access pre-emptible GPU hours at some low price. Let’s say that low price is $6/GB300/hour. If the inference wrapper can achieve demand of some base load of, equivalent of a rack of GB300s (72 GPUs). Essentially, the wrapper can route baseload traffic to the primary provider at market API prices (and make no money). But when the cheap GPUs are available, they can route them to the hosted instances to internalize the API margins. DeepSeek’s team has an estimate of ~$36/gpu/hour of monetization for DeepSeek 4.1 flash at off peak rates. So this team would be making $(36-6)/gpu/hour for any traffic they can route to the cheap GPUs. —- But from an user standpoint… In many ways, inference APIs should be validated like a trusted actor end to end. comments.author: kdavis
comments.text: Interesting. I've only read the abstract, but... - It seems strange to get an algebra of Type I for a QFT. Generally one would expect an algebra of Type II when including gravity. Maybe it's a result of a finite G and not the infinitesimal G that gives Type II? - It seems like it would take some care to construct a Lorentzian path integral rigorously. I wonder how that was done. - I wonder how background independence is being claimed while at the same time quantizing on intersecting null cones. The definition of the null cones is a background.

comments.author: hecmmm
comments.text: Abstract: We propose a background independent quantization of vacuum general relativity on four dimensional Lorentzian spacetimes. Starting from first order gravity, we solve the gravitational constraints on intersecting null cones of a bulk subregion and obtain the reduced phase space at finite GN. We promote its canonical Poisson brackets to commutation relations and use deformations of the reduced action to define an algebra of observables. Equipped with this, we use Gaussian wavefunctions of canonical pairs to construct a nonperturbative Hilbert space representation, for which this algebra generates a type I factor. By composing amplitudes between states prepared on null cones, we then obtain a Lorentzian path integral in which each sum over intermediate states converges absolutely. As a check, we compute the amplitude for graviton pair creation and annihilation on a null cone nonperturbatively in GN and find a finite closed form expression, even though expanding first in GN yields a logarithmic divergence. We next use diffeomorphism invariance of the path integral to show that a macroscopic causal diamond with a given maximum size has a finite dimensional Hilbert space. From the Lorentzian trace we obtain the Bekenstein Hawking entropy for marginally trapped surfaces and calculate its logarithmic correction for large Schwarzschild black holes, recovering at one loop the coefficient Sen obtained through Euclidean methods. We end by deriving the semiclassical Einstein equations to one loop as the low energy limit of this theory.

Instead of pasting what I’ve found out, which is too nuanced to be contained in an HN comment and will inevitably tainted by my own biases, I would strongly recommend folks to pose their favorite chatbot(s) this very neutral prompt: “Impact of USAID on the average US taxpayer as supported by evidence and empirical studies” Note it does not specify if the impact is good or bad, and explicitly demands evidence, which I’ve found is generally the best way to get all sides of the issue. comments.author: andai
comments.text: Cool. I like the swiping. Very satisfying. I made my own flashcard thing a few months ago, when I realized my goal was the opposite of Anki's goal. Anki — and all flashcard software these days — makes learning as efficient as possible, which they define as minimizing learning time. It does this by showing you things as rarely as possible. Unfortunately that also maximizes pain, effort and forgetting, and minimizes fluency. I wanted the opposite of that, because I am lazy and don't like effort, pain and failure. (I also like fluency!) The goal of minimizing time makes sense for a law student or someone in med school, but for me that's not a problem I actually have, and it creates all these other problems. (Flashcard software is also known to have pretty bad user retention, which if I had to guess is due to the fact that it is effectively designed to be painful.) So I just made a thing oriented around the exact opposite goal: showing me cards as often as possible! (And turns out I was half a century late with this idea :) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precision_teaching Then I realized I could just modify Anki instead of maintaining an entire software, so I did that instead. Then I realized I am just too lazy to do flashcards, and creating new software did not solve that problem. To make the reps easy and to maximize fluency. (The quest continues... maybe I should try again when I get some Ritalin!) p.s. I did a deep dive on this stuff and discovered that what we call "overlearning" is actually just what used to be called learning not so long ago, and that what we call "mastery learning" is actually temporary basic competence .

Everyone was making these devices using incredibly expensive materials and low throughput techniques, but the only way the technology could be viable commercially was for it to be extremely cheap. IIRC there was one paper that calculated that the devices has to be as cheap as carpet to be worthwhile. Granted, I was a pretty obnoxious twenty-something, but it didn't make me popular to point this out to my fellow researchers.

comments.author: tptacek
comments.text: This is the single most important attack vector for SAAS companies. It has been for a long time --- this is the standard fact pattern for every SAAS breach --- but much more so today. As the number of employees grow, the likelihood that one of their laptops will get compromised approaches 1. When that happens, the attacker will be able to push code to Github, and if that code gets deployed, you're owned. In 1Password's case, the absolute worst-case catastrophe is mitigated by the fact that customers retain custody of their unlocking secrets; 1Password (at least in the normal product flows) simply doesn't hold it. But an attack like this implicates every catastrophe short of that worst case. Change velocity in 2026 is unreal and that trend is going to continue. You could not outcompete 1Password by building a handcrafted artisanal password manager backend (witness all the commercially successful password managers that don't even share 1Password's customer secret custody model). You have to accept insane PR rates as a premise to do modern SAAS security. So the question then becomes: what is review? It's not what r/programming assumes it is; you almost certainly can't literally have a team of people line-by-line reviewing PRs anymore, at least not across the whole codebase (you can and should probably do a threat model for your codebase and institute stuff like that on a case-by-case basis, though). What you can realistically expect to review for is change provenance; a human developer signoff of some sort. But it's tricky! The attacker owns your email during the window of attack. I think this is a fun problem to noodle on, and someone could probably come up with something here that would make a real difference.

comments.author: ChrisHardie
comments.text: Longtime 1Password user here who maintains a local-only vault (and is therefore stuck on older versions of their apps/extensions) out of concern for incidents like this. But "malicious actor pushes code to production services" seems like exactly the foundation for someone to eventually insert themselves into the middle of a user's access to decrypted vault contents. I really wish 1Password would return to supporting local-only vaults.

comments.text: That was my experience, too. One of my pet projects is experimenting with various bots for a niche board game. At some point, I had the idea to try a transformer. Fable 5.2 wrote a bug-ridden training pipeline that just wasn't able to get the loss down, and the transformer-based bot didn't play well. Then I asked Gemini to review the implementation. It found many bugs and fixed all of them. The next training run produced good results, and the transformer-based bot was the best of all my bots. My take: we really need good open-weight models. People should collect their Claude Code/Codex/AGY/... logs and be ready to eventually donate them to train open-weight models. Another take: Anthropic could likely release much better models, but they struggle to make them selectively weak, like they did with Fable without making them weak overall. EDIT: The bot transformer wasn't a LLM, just 200k params input: history of all players moves output: probability distribution over next possible moves
